data.name: Street Heat
data.detailed_description:
Surrender your senses to the ultimate top-down racing experience! Street Heat is an action-packed four-player party-piece enhanced by vibrant neon-noir visuals and a masterful ’80s soundtrack. Go bumper-to-bumper with three other racers as you screech around corners, hurtle over deadly jumps and floor it across busy train tracks in the race for the checkered flag.

Pick your car and livery of choice and get racing against friends, strangers or AI within seconds. But beware: spin off the track’s edge or get obliterated by the trains and your race is over until the next round!

Features

• Fiercely competitive arcade racing: Trade paint as you push your competition off the track and scrape your way to first place in fast and frantic four-player races.
• Flexible online multiplayer: Simultaneously take on friends and strangers both locally and online via matchmaking that supports multiple local players.
• Challenging AI: Fancy offline tussles? Whether playing solo or with a friend or two, fill in the spare slots with AI racers and tweak their skill settings to ensure a competitive race every time.
• Randomized hazards: With slippery oil slicks and deadly train carriages roaring through Street Heat’s twisting cityscapes, no two races are the same. And with no respawns available, every corner could be your last!
• Tournament play: Participate in multi-race events where points are awarded for finishing positions, fastest laps and kills.
• Track voting system: Everybody gets a say in which track’s up next via a post-race ballot.
• Steam Achievements
• Full controller support
• Steam Cloud support

data.short_description: Four-player arcade racing with a sensational synthwave soundtrack! Take to city streets in local or online mutiplayer and race across hazardous tracks. Boasting an unbelievably satisfying handling model, Street Heat will have you punching the air as you master its seat-of-your-pants drift physics.

highlighted.name: Wasn't I Supposed to Do That?

reviews.review:
Street Heat is a top-down arcade racing game that trades realistic driving for drifting, collisions, dangerous obstacles, and the kind of unpredictable competition that works especially well with a group of friends. Developed by Astalo Games and published by PQube, it leans heavily into a neon-drenched retro atmosphere inspired by the 1980s. Instead of overwhelming the player with vehicle tuning or complicated racing systems, the game focuses on immediately understandable action where staying on the track can be just as important as reaching the finish line first.

Driving is intentionally loose and energetic. Cars slide readily around corners, so learning how to control a drift is central to maintaining speed. The handling is accessible enough for newcomers to start racing quickly, but there is still satisfaction in discovering how early to initiate a turn and how aggressively to accelerate out of it. Because the action is viewed from above, players can usually see upcoming corners and nearby competitors, yet the speed of the races means there is rarely much time to plan. A seemingly comfortable lead can disappear after one badly timed turn.

The tracks make that danger considerably more interesting. Street Heat includes hazards such as oil slicks, moving trains, jumps, and areas where careless driving can send a vehicle out of contention. Randomized obstacles help make repeated races less predictable, forcing players to react instead of relying entirely on memorized routines. Most importantly, there are no convenient mid-round respawns after being eliminated. A major crash can end the current race, which adds genuine consequences to risky driving. Attempting an ambitious shortcut or forcing another racer toward danger can create a major advantage, but the same maneuver can easily eliminate the attacker.

Contact between competitors plays an important role in this risk-and-reward system. Players can bump, block, and pressure opponents instead of simply concentrating on the fastest racing line. This creates an enjoyable contrast between clean driving and deliberate aggression. Sometimes the smartest choice is to stay away from a chaotic fight and protect a strong position. At other times, knocking a rival into a hazard can be more valuable than shaving a fraction of a second from a lap. The result is a racing game where tactical opportunism matters alongside basic driving ability.

Multiplayer is the strongest part of the package. Up to four racers can compete, with local and online multiplayer options giving groups several ways to play together. Empty positions can be filled by AI-controlled opponents, and adjustable AI difficulty makes the game reasonably approachable when human competitors are unavailable. Solo play is therefore possible, but the design becomes much more entertaining when several people are fighting for position. Human unpredictability complements the hazards especially well, turning small mistakes and aggressive maneuvers into memorable moments.

Tournament events add some structure beyond isolated races. Points can be earned through finishing positions, fastest laps, and kills, meaning success is not determined exclusively by conventional racing performance. A player who is particularly aggressive may still contribute strongly through eliminations, while someone focused on precision can pursue quick laps and consistent finishes. Players can also vote for upcoming tracks, which is a sensible feature for a party-oriented game and keeps groups involved between races.

Visually, Street Heat establishes a clear identity through glowing streets, colorful cars, dark urban surroundings, and an unmistakable neon aesthetic. It is not attempting photorealism, and that works in its favor. The stylized presentation remains readable from the overhead perspective while giving the races plenty of personality. Synthwave music completes the retro atmosphere and fits naturally with the rapid pace. Vehicle liveries provide an additional degree of personalization without distracting from the straightforward arcade structure.

The biggest weakness is limited depth for players seeking a substantial single-player racing experience. There is no elaborate career structure or deep simulation system driving long-term progression. Its appeal instead comes from replaying short, competitive races and enjoying how different hazards and opponents alter each encounter. The elimination rules can also be unforgiving. Crashing early means sitting out until the following round, which creates tension but can occasionally interrupt the fun, particularly when a mistake happens almost immediately.

Steam Deck compatibility is currently listed as Unknown rather than carrying an official Valve Verified or Playable rating. The modest system requirements and controller-focused design may make the game a reasonable candidate for portable play, but the absence of an official compatibility classification means Steam Deck users should not assume completely trouble-free operation based solely on the Windows version.

Street Heat ultimately works best when approached as a compact party racer rather than a feature-heavy racing simulation. Its drifting, destructive competition, environmental hazards, elimination mechanics, tournament scoring, local multiplayer, and online support create an entertaining foundation for short sessions. The amount of long-term content is comparatively modest, but the combination of simple controls and unpredictable racing gives it an enjoyable pick-up-and-play quality. Players looking for neon arcade racing with an emphasis on chaos and friendly competition will find its strongest qualities immediately apparent.

Rating: 7/10
